blocks.text: EEG test measures the electrical activity of brain. Its basic principle is based on detecting the electrical nerve impulses being transmitted among the neurons.

Procedure: During EEG, metal electrodes are attached to the scalp. These electrodes are connected to an amplifier. The amplifier magnifies the electrical signals detected by the electrodes. The signals are then recorded and displayed as a series of waveforms on a computer screen or paper.

blocks.alt: A head with many electrodes attached to the scalp, their wires gathered together, and beside it a sheet of wavy traces labelled EEG reading.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.22: Electroencephalography (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.22).

blocks.text: Uses: EEG is done to evaluate various neurological conditions, including seizures, epilepsy, and brain tumors. It is painless and does not require sedation or anaesthesia.

blocks.title: For Information
blocks.text:
Each wave of EEG is associated with different states of brain activity.
• Gamma waves are associated with high perception, learning, problem-solving activities.
• Beta waves are associated with normal alert state and active thinking.
• Alpha waves show physically and mentally relaxed state.
• Theta waves show deep sleep (dreams and reduced consciousness).
• Delta waves show deepest sleep and dreaming.

blocks.alt: Five EEG wave traces in coloured bands: Gamma (fastest, smallest), Beta, Alpha, Theta and Delta (slowest, largest). From gamma to delta the waves become slower and taller.
blocks.caption: EEG waves (original drawing after the waveforms in the textbook's 'For Information' box on EEG).
